question: In recent weeks, a number of Member States have experienced a surge in fuel retail prices, which in some cases appears to be more pronounced than the rise in international crude oil prices.

Data published in the Commission’s weekly Oil Bulletin, together with the ARA (Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp) refined product benchmarks, point to a non-linear passthrough of Brent oil price changes throughout the refining and distribution chain at times.

The EU fuel market is subject to the competition rules laid down in Articles 101 and 102 TFEU, and to the energy market monitoring framework provided for in Regulation (EU) No 1227/2011 (REMIT), aimed at preventing market manipulation and abuse of information. Consequently, any asymmetrical price transmission or abnormal margins could create distortions that harm consumers and businesses. In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission have up-to-date analyses of how margins have evolved throughout the oil supply chain and the extent to which current prices are consistent with global benchmarks?

Does it believe that it would be appropriate to launch checks or investigations, including through the EU Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators and the national competition authorities, to identify any speculation or anti-competitive practices?
What measures will it take to increase transparency and price monitoring throughout the fuel supply chain in the EU?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2026) The Commission tracks energy prices and produces a weekly Oil Bulletin and considers other market analysis such as product specific imbalances and refining capacities and constraints.

Under the Regulation on Wholesale Energy Market Integrity and Transparency (REMIT)1 national authorities are responsible for enforcement against market abusive behaviour as regards wholesale energy products in electricity, natural gas and hydrogen. REMIT does not cover mineral oil markets.

The Commission and national competition authorities may initiate a competition investigation where there are indications of either anti-competitive agreements (Article 101 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU)) or abuse of a dominant position (Article 102 TFEU) affecting trade between Member States.

While atypical pricing may merit examination, a disparity between input costs and retail prices alone is not as such and taken in isolation, indicative of a potential breach of EU competition rules. However, certain national practices in pricing fuel may breach other EU rules.

Against this background, the Commission launched, on 29 April 2026, infringement proceedings against Hungary and Slovakia for the introduction of measures discriminating between EU citizens when fuelling vehicles2. As a result, Slovakia has since lifted the discriminatory fuel measures. The Commission will continue monitoring the evolution of the crisis and assessing its potential impacts.

To address the impacts of the disruption of oil and gas transit, the Commission put forward on 22 April 2026 its new initiative AccelerateEU3, proposing timely, targeted and temporary measures to bring relief to consumers, while avoiding fragmented national responses.
